Calls for tighter availability restrictions have been countered by fears they could make treatment unaffordable for many pet owners. Limiting the availability of parasite treatments at the centre of an environmental row may not be enough to prevent harmful impacts, a senior VMD official has conceded. The admission, made during evidence to a House of Lords inquiry, follows one veterinary organisation’s call for products containing fipronil and imidacloprid to be reclassified as prescription only (POM-V). But other senior clinicians and industry figures have warned the approach could prove “price restrictive” for many pet owners seeking treatment. Medicine regulators are currently considering measures that would restrict the availability of products containing fipronil and imidacloprid to vets, pharmacists and other suitably qualified persons (SQPs). Officials argue the plan, which emerged when the Government’s pharmaceutical in the environment group issued a call for evidence in April, would ensure consumers received professional advice on appropriate usage at point of sale. But former RCVS president Lord Trees raised concerns about the potential risks from online sales during the latest evidence session of the Lords’ environment and climate change committee probe on 23 June. He described a “mystery shopper” exercise undertaken by the committee where a product containing one of the chemicals under scrutiny, imidacloprid, was purchased without usage guidance, prescription or any indication of what an SQP may have said or done prior to the sale being completed. He asked: “Do you think that’s a satisfactory way of distributing products which are potentially quite harmful to the environment?”. VMD chief executive Abi Seager acknowledged there was a need to review distribution categories, but argued that was part of the call for evidence, which closed last month. She added: “In answer to your question, no, we don’t think necessarily it’s sufficient, which is why we’re asking more broadly for evidence to support us looking into that.” The exchange followed a submission to the call for evidence by the Progressive Veterinary Association (PVA), which claimed POM-V designation was a “minimum” requirement. It argued the present proposals were unlikely to prevent online sales occurring without appropriate advice being given. But while the merits of reassessing both current distribution categories and point-of-purchase advice were recognised, senior figures who gave evidence during earlier committee sessions voiced concerns about the potential consequences of tighter restrictions. European Scientific Counsel Companion Animal Parasites (ESCCAP) chairperson Ian Wright said: “I think making these products POM-V only would be a price-restrictive issue for many pet owners.” BVA senior vice-president Elizabeth Mullineaux also suggested a market shift was needed to make the products more affordable, though she acknowledged they would be prescription only “in an ideal world”. Meanwhile, NOAH deputy chief executive Donal Murphy insisted effective parasite control remained “a key part” of the responsibility to keep pets healthy and safe. But the PVA submission questioned whether routine or subscription-based parasiticide use represented best practice and warned commercial considerations “must not override” either that or broader environmental obligations. It added: “The evidence that companion animal treatments contribute to environmental loading is now sufficiently robust to require urgent regulatory intervention.” However, Environment Agency chief scientist Robert Bradburne told the committee the organisation had “no strong evidence of cause and effect” on the invertebrate population, a key aspect of environmental concerns to date, despite the chemicals being present at levels where impacts would be anticipated. title: Gonzalez v. Department of Homeland Security - ACLU of Illinois
content: Under the second Trump Administration, the Department of Homeland Security has engaged in excessive, violent and reckless immigration activities, resulting in thousands of people being taken into custody.  Many of these individuals have been held in inhumane conditions for months. But DHS has continued to harm even those released from custody by refusing to return personal property ICE (a part of DHS) seized when it took them into custody.  When the government obtains someone’s property, it must return those items when its interest in them expires, even if it initially took control of the items lawfully. DHS routinely flouts this obligation. It has adopted a de facto policy of keeping property seized from people it detained for civil immigration purposes long after any plausible governmental interest in the items expired. This case challenges DHS’s conduct on behalf of seven people and a class of similarly situated individuals. ICE detained each of the named plaintiffs, stripped them of important property, and failed to return their items months after their release. ICE failed to return Employment Authorization Documents and other important documents, along with items such as cell phones and car keys. As a result, the plaintiffs have lost work opportunities, feared going out in public (because they don’t have identification, which could lead ICE to detain them again), and suffered other forms of personal and economic hardship. The plaintiffs bring this case to regain the items DHS withheld from them and ensure that the agency comports with its legal duties when handling property in the future. We are pleased to partner in this case, filed in the federal district court in the District of Columbia, with the ACLU of DC, Democracy Defenders Fund, Platkin LLC, and Wilkie Farr & Gallagher LLP. Controversy over the state’s attempt to participate in a federal nuclear energy program has highlighted rifts in state and local officials’ perspectives on the role West Virginia could play in the nuclear energy space, and signaled that West Virginia’s motivation to pursue nuclear energy could be quite fragile. “Soaring electricity demand threatens to lock in decades of fossil fuel dependence.” Why this is important: The article highlights that the growth in the demand for electricity that is being driven by data centers is, by consequence, causing accelerated growth in natural gas-fired power plant development and continued support for a fossil fuel-based economy. Specifically, the article notes that by 2030, over 60,000 Megawatts of new natural gas-based power plants – which translates to about 100 units – are scheduled to be online. In addition, older coal-fired power plants that may have otherwise not been economical to continue operating are in fact needed to meet new demand. At the same time, because of their variable nature and comparatively lower capacity, planned solar and wind power additions have decreased. The article laments the environmental harms and adverse health impacts of continuing long-term reliance on fossil fuels versus a transition to cleaner and more sustainable power. But the upshot is that the so-called “Dominant Model” of U.S. energy policy, which is founded largely on the economic value of fossil fuel reliance, is remaining intact as a result of the data center-driven growth in electric demand. --- Derrick Price Williamson Why Microgrids are Essential Building Blocks in Future U.S. Electric Grid “The Office of Electricity’s Microgrid Research and Development Program shows that well-designed microgrids can provide both the flexibility in deployment and usability through a ‘Microgrid Building Block’ concept.” Why this is important: While there are extensive benefits to the wide-scale availability of electricity from the larger grid, there are detriments when portions of that grid are disrupted by weather or other events. During those times, the article discusses the benefits of microgrids that can be designed for flexibility and quick deployment. Instead of a single microgrid, the "Microgrid Building Blocks" approach connects individual modules of a microgrid with one another to create larger power systems to fit the needs of a specific circumstance.

Beyond the benefit of flexible and faster deployment in the event that portions of the larger grid go down, the article also discusses that this building block concept could allow large loads like data centers to begin operations more quickly by deploying sufficient power supply faster than the larger grid could provide. At this time, the Microgrid Building Block approach appears conceptual on a large scale, but with the increasing need for generation and capacity on the larger grid, this approach is likely an option that will be investigated further in the coming years. --- Steven W. Lee The World has Nearly Burned Through Its Oil Stockpile Buffer, Executives Say “Governments and energy companies have drawn oil from stockpiles to alleviate pressure in a global oil market facing unprecedented supply disruptions this year due to the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.” Why this is important: Since the beginning of this year, due to the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, more than 1 billion barrels of oil have been released mainly from onshore commercial inventories. The International Energy Agency, the coordinator of the West’s strategic oil reserves, is negotiating for 100 million barrels of crude and diesel to be released in order to assist in alleviating soaring diesel prices. For scale, the world oil demand is about 102 million barrels per day. According to the article, Chevron executives believe that it will take years to refill oil inventories on top of meeting the already huge demand. This creates the need to build additional inventories around the globe. --- Taiesha K. Morgan US has More Natural Gas than It Can Use as War Chokes Global Supply “Soaring gas production is poised to bolster US manufacturing, creating an economic tailwind.” Why this is important: While natural gas around the world is in short supply due to the Iran war, at the moment the United States actually has an oversupply of natural gas in Texas tied to oil production. In the Permian Basin in Texas, a need to produce oil has resulted in natural gas producers paying customers to take gas that comes out of the ground at the same time. On April 24, the gas price was -$9.60. This imbalance is predicted to be short-lived, as by the end of the year, new gas pipelines will come online that will take this gas out of the basin into markets where it can be sold. According to the article, those events may also help lower energy prices in the U.S. --- Mark E. Heath US Approves Construction Permit for First Commercial SMR “The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission has granted a construction permit to the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) for a small modular nuclear reactor (SMR) at its Clinch River site in Oak Ridge, Tennessee.” Why this is important: Small nuclear reactors (SMRs) have made the energy news in recent years for their ability to be modularly developed at a smaller scale and deployed more quickly than larger nuclear reactors. Despite the general nuclear renaissance to address rising energy needs, the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) only recently approved the first commercial SMR project in Tennessee, and only one other SMR currently in operation in the world is in Russia. As noted in the article, while SMR technology is still in its nascent stages, this is a major milestone for the new nuclear technology to be part of the solution of growing energy demand. ﻿--- Steven W. Lee Energy Secretary Promotes Coal Investment During North Carolina Visit “Energy Secretary Chris Wright highlighted federal upgrades at Duke’s Roxboro coal plant as rising power demand puts electricity costs and pollution in focus.” Why this is important: U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright visited Duke Power’s Roxboro coal-fired electrical generation plant recently to promote the use of federal funds to upgrade existing coal-fired electrical generation even when the plants are set to retire. The funds are designed to continue electrical production while potential replacements are being built. In June, the North Carolina coal-fired plant built in 1966, which had been set to retire, received $28.4 million in federal funds to make repairs. The coal-fired plant will eventually be replaced in 2028 by natural gas units under construction. As noted in the article, the Trump administration is using federal grants to retain aging coal-fired electricity plants to avoid shortages of electricity in times when data centers and other industries have very high electrical demands. --- Mark E. Heath Tesla is Now Making More EVs that can Double as a Home Battery “While other vehicle-to-home systems rely on customers installing pricey bidirectional chargers, Tesla embeds the power-conversion hardware in the cars themselves.” Why this is important: While vehicle-to-home backup power systems usually require a device to convert direct current from the vehicle to home-ready alternating current, the article highlights that Tesla has created an exception with its Cybertruck. The Cybertruck is the only vehicle with the ability to send AC power to homes and the grid, but Tesla has announced that it is expanding the ability to the new Model 3 and Model Y electric vehicles. This could mitigate high up-front costs in purchasing electric vehicles. This technology development could allow for electric vehicles to be used as backup batteries and grid assets. A recent study found that California could get one-third of its grid energy storage needs from just 10 percent of the 9.7 million electric vehicles it expects to have by the mid-2030s. That said, only California and Maryland have established regulations that allow this bidirectional charging outside of the pilot projects, which have used this technology for decades. Tesla has partnered with Pacific Gas & Electric, California’s largest utility, and Texas’ CenterPoint Energy and Oncor, allowing Cybertrucks to tap their battery power to send back to the grids. --- Taiesha K. title: One Big Thing Connects Sam Alito’s Recent Comments About Roe v. Wade and the “Cornell Seven” - Slate

Enter your email to receive alerts for this author. Sign in or create an account to better manage your email preferences. Are you sure you want to unsubscribe from email alerts for Dahlia Lithwick? Sign up for Executive Dysfunction, a weekly newsletter that highlights one under-the-radar story about how Trump is changing the law—or how the law is pushing back—and keeps you posted on the latest from Slate’s Jurisprudence team. The alleged gang rape scandal that continues to unfold at Cornell University serves as yet another reminder that the legal system puts structures into place that should ostensibly protect women from being drugged, assaulted, and gaslit, and yet it persistently fails to manage any of the above. On this week’s Amicus podcast, Dahlia Lithwick spoke about the myriad ways in which the legal system cannot meet the moment with respect to women, with Julie Suk, the Leonard F. Manning professor of law at Fordham University. Suk’s scholarship focuses on the processes of constitutional amendment and reform and the feminist constitutional movements. Her most recent book, The Shadow Court: Rescuing Democracy From the Supreme Court, was published last month and attempts to reclaim the constitutional system for the people. A portion of their conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity below. Dahlia Lithwick: So much of the work you’ve done has been rooted in this idea that our legal structures, in some ways by design, have always failed and continue to fail women and vulnerable communities. We’re in a moment where the shadow of this Cornell case is hanging so heavy. We’re watching another generation of young women—who maybe didn’t live through #MeToo and Epstein Island and Christine Blasey Ford—who are just looking around at the Cornell story and saying, “Where is the law? How are we moving backward instead of forward?” What do you have to say about this moment? Julie Suk: It seems at a basic level we did not have criminal law—or the administrative structures of a university in the Cornell case—remedying, giving justice to, or creating conditions under which Jane Doe could actually continue her education. She left the school after the trauma, to which there was no institutional response. I think the problem in this case tracks what I argue in After Misogyny, which is that the legal structure is connected to a culture which basically enforces the overentitlement of men to women’s forbearance and sacrifices. If you look at all of those Snapchat messages in the fraternity in the Cornell case, the concept of “free pussy”—pardon my language, but I think those were the words—the very concept is We are entitled. Here it is. Take what you’re entitled to. And that connects to a legal system that does not recognize the overentitlement of men to women’s sacrifices, forbearance, and pain. It’s not just in the gender violence or nonconsensual sex settings. There’s a similar dynamic societally, where we ban abortion because the society is overentitled to women’s sacrifices for the public good, so childbearing and child-rearing become entitlements too. And the law just doesn’t recognize that as a problem. That’s just our baseline set of entitlements. That’s why the law fails. I’m not saying we would have to go to a different standard with regard to consent in criminal rape law. I think there are a lot of different ways and different bodies of law that could respond to this overentitlement problem. I think the public debate has really focused in this case on the question of whether the criminal law failed. I don’t have a strong view on whether or not I think the criminal law should change because of this case. Instead, it’s worth looking at things that seem much more attenuated from the facts of this concrete case. It’s shocking but not surprising that the overentitlement dynamic, which I call misogyny, takes over. The way that social life is structured in universities, because of choices that are made about not recognizing fraternities, or choices that are made about drinking in dorms; a whole bunch of choices that—at least in terms of male-dominated spaces like fraternities—entitlement takes over because the universities generally say, “Well, the fraternities are not part of us, so we’re not responsible,” or, “That’s not within our jurisdiction exactly.” We need to start thinking not just about the criminal law, but the way in which we structure the institutions where opportunities are distributed, in which inequalities are perpetuated, as social spaces that need to be restructured so that the overentitlement of men to women’s bodies, to women’s forbearance, to women’s reproductive labor—all of those things have to be rethought. I don’t have a simple criminal law answer to all that, but so much of what I want to do in my work as a law professor and as a political theorist is think about the way that new and different institutions can empower people who are not currently empowered. ﻿Last week, Justice Samuel Alito gave an interview to Jan Crawford of CBS about his new book. And in that interview he discussed why he thinks it unlikely the court will overturn the marriage equality decision, Obergefell. He essentially said that Obergefell is safe because Americans have a reliance interest in it. People structured their lives around that liberty. Crawford pointed out that a lot of people felt they also had a reliance interest in Roe v. Wade, that “people thought that, that Roe was settled law of the land, and obviously there were consequences when the court overturned Roe and Casey.” And to that Justice Alito responded: “After Obergefell, people of the same sex got married and entered into contracts, and so there was much, it was much more concrete.” He went on to say that “The argument was made that it had an effect on people’s ideas, women’s ideas about the kind of society they were going to live in. This would have an effect on society. It was much more abstract than what would’ve been involved had we been asked to overturn Obergefell.” I think what he’s saying is that women’s reliance interests in Roe for 50 years were abstractions to him, whereas there were concrete, meaningful decisions made in reliance on Obergefell. You know as well as I do how many amicus briefs were written in Dobbs that laid out the ways in which women were making economic, health, and other choices in reliance on Roe. This is such an interesting commentary on what is visible to justices and what isn’t. I find it quite astonishing in 2026 to hear a justice of the Supreme Court say that women’s reliance interests on the right to abortion were “abstract.” I think that comes from a set of beliefs about what women really want. Part of the way the law fails women is through the narrative that what I’m calling “overentitlement” is actually in line with what everyone wants and is consenting to. And beyond consenting to, that affirms that entitlement. So if you think of childbearing and child-rearing as women’s destiny, and not just destiny, but women’s will, then it’s not a stretch to say the very idea that you relied on Roe to make these choices was abstract. It’s just to say you don’t really believe that the possibility of having an abortion would play that much of a role in whether and when you went to school and trained yourself for a certain career and so forth, in the same way that people, especially men, get married and then form all kinds of other economic decisions based on marriage. So I do think that part of it is not just about being out of touch with lived experience, but also a completely different understanding of the baseline as consented, a completely different understanding of what is natural and embraced by everyone, as compared to another story you could tell, which is we have a bunch of structures that assume and enforce the notion that women make sacrifices for the public good and they are undercompensated or not compensated. If you tell that story, then everything that follows will also be different. Slate is published by The Slate

title: Obituary information for Richard V. Massey - Solimine Funeral Home
content: Richard Vincent Massey, age 88 of Swampscott, MA and Oldsmar, Fl, passed away peacefully on Tuesday, October 6, 2026.  Born in Swampscott, MA, he was the son of the late John and Gertrude (Carpenter) Massey.  Dick was the devoted husband of the late Johanne (Andersen) Massey with whom he shared 44 years of marriage. He was a lifelong resident of Swampscott, graduating from Swampscott High School with the class of 1956.  Growing up on the hill with his many friends, he was an exceptional athlete, greatly enjoying the camaraderie of his friends and teammates.  Following his high school graduation, Dick took his talents to Saint Lawrence University where he was a key player on the 1961 National Championship runner-up hockey team.  After college, the now married Dick and Johanne came home to Swampscott where he began work at Massey Plumbing & Heating Co., which today is recognized as the oldest continuously operating business in Swampscott.  During his post college time, Dick played in the New England Hockey League and refereed High School Hockey with his family in tow for many memorable moments.  As the first coach for Swampscott Youth Hockey, he was instrumental in the program’s inception.  Dick was recognized for his athletic achievements and contributions with his election to The Swampscott High School Athletic Hall of Fame. From summers in Ossipee, NH, spring trips to Oldsmar, FLA, winters skiing at Sugarloaf, ME, golfing around the North Shore and membership at Tedesco Country Club and Fox Hollow, The Massey Family could not have had a better upbringing.  In retirement, Dick enjoyed his time between Swampscott, MA and Oldsmar, FL, living his life well lived. His legacy is carried on through his four-(4) sons and their families; Rick and Ann Massey of Swampscott, MA; Michael and Cara Massey of Swampscott, MA; Peter and Kelly Massey of Lynn, MA; and, Jeff Massey of Swampscott, MA; six-(6) grandchildren; Brendan and Julia Massey; Justin Massey and his wife Hypatia and Trevor Massey; Alyson Massey; and Adeline Massey; and his three-(3) great-grandchildren; Ezme and Chase Massey; and Aria Massey. For the past decade he found comfort in the loving companionship of Claire Kirk and her family; Deborah Kirk of Swampscott, MA; Mike and Shawna Kirk and family of Beverly, MA; Kevin and Kim Kirk and family of Matthews, NC. Dick was a proud brother to his sister Donna Massey of Natick, MA; the late John “Jack” Massey who is survived by his wife Jif of San Clemente, CA; and the late Anne (Massey) Burnham who is survived by her husband Charlie of Stafford, NH. He was the son-in-law of the late Ty and Eleanor Andersen of Swampscott; brother-in-law to Ty and Deborah Andersen of Lakeland Fla; and to the late Dean Andersen of Swampscott, MA. title: Cervantes v. Bianco - League of Women Voters of California
content: The League of Women Voters of California (LWVC) joined a legal challenge (Cervantes v. Bianco) urging the California Supreme Court to take swift and decisive action to address the unlawful seizure of ballots from the 2025 special election by the Riverside County (CA) sheriff. Sheriff Bianco claimed the seizure was necessary to investigate potential irregularities in the November 2025 vote, but as CalMatters detailed, these unproven claims were the result of a years-long campaign by groups aligned with the “constitutional sheriff” movement pressuring the sheriff to intervene in local elections. On September 24, 2026, the California Supreme Court unanimously ruled against Bianco, holding that state law unambiguously prohibits law enforcement from removing ballots from the custody of election officials, and ordered the materials returned. In a unanimous opinion, the California Supreme Court rules the sheriff’s seizure of the ballots was unlawful and orders him to return them to the custody of Riverside County election officials. The California Supreme Court hears oral arguments in two lawsuits challenging the sheriff’s seizure of the ballots. In the case of Bonta v. Bianco, the California Supreme Court ordered the pause of the Sheriff’s “investigation.” Represented by Campaign Legal Center, the LWVC joined Common Cause to file an amicus brief in the California Supreme Court supporting the petitioners. Several Riverside County voters file a lawsuit in the California Supreme Court, asserting the investigation was illegal under several California laws and requesting the immediate return of the seized ballots to county election officials. Alleging a “criminal investigation,” Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco seized almost 650,000 ballots for the November 2025 election. Prop 50 was on the ballot, a contest in which voters decisively agreed to pause the state’s independent redistricting commission and add five additional Democratic seats. title: Hall of Famers v bunch of gamers: the Dodgers’ exit proves money can’t buy everything - The Guardian
content: The Brewers turned LA’s stars into ghosts during their four-game NLCS sweep, destroying the ‘team that destroyed baseball’ and revealing the sport’s hard truth Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy had just watched his club dismantle Los Angeles for a fourth straight National League Championship Series game. Standing with his team in the Dodger Stadium clubhouse, he was ready to celebrate. But before popping his champagne and setting off a stream of celebratory suds, Murphy had a message. “They got a bunch of Hall of Famers. We got a bunch of gamers.” Murphy had nailed the Dodgers to the wall, ending the season of a juggernaut who came into 2026 with eyes on becoming the first NL team to win three straight World Series titles. The Dodgers are dead, and instead, it’s Milwaukee who made history, becoming the first team to avenge an NLCS sweep by returning the favor against that very same team, the very next season. Making history, it seems, is a theme with these Brewers, who racked up a franchise-best 103 wins during the regular season, and have now dethroned a team who seemed a shoo-in to become baseball’s first true dynasty since the millennium. Milwaukee transformed LA into a team of ghosts, and no more so than in Game 4. With the desperate Dodgers bidding to wake up the echoes with a 4-0 lead, the Brewers went to work. And again, it was Jake Bauers who broke LA’s back. In Game 2, Bauers tortured Dodgers ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto with an epic 12-pitch walk that sparked a key rally. In Game 3, there was an epic 11-pitch at-bat, this time against two-time Cy Young Award winner Blake Snell, concluding with a franchise-defining home run. In the fourth inning of Game 4, Bauers struck a double against starter Tyler Glasnow, cutting the Dodgers’ lead in half. An inning later, Bauers – the journeyman infielder who paused his retirement and returned this season because he needed health insurance for his soon-to-be newborn – drew a bases-loaded walk to tie the game. Garrett Mitchell’s sixth-inning solo home run gave Milwaukee a lead that would hold up. An old-school, three-inning save by Aaron Ashby was the chef’s kiss. Now Milwaukee will head to their first World Series since 1982. There will be plenty of time to ply the Brew Crew with pixelated plaudits as they await their American League opponents, the Tampa Bay Rays or Cleveland Guardians. First, though, comes the funeral. The tight, young, dynamic and fundamentally sound Brewers made Los Angeles’s best look old, flat and incapable. And while it all seems somewhat sudden, perhaps the writing was on the wall all along. The Dodgers, the team who have everything, lack for nothing and have more money than Davy Crockett, won 100 games this season, but were just 38-37 against teams above .500 and hit into an MLB-worst 128 double-plays. In ways, they looked more like another expensive but deeply flawed coastal superpower: the New York Yankees. The Bronx bombs also beat up on lesser opponents all season long while struggling against higher-end teams. It’s no coincidence that both teams are now out; baseball has a way of weeding out the suckers, even in what some believe is a “crap shoot” of a postseason. Perhaps the most shocking spectacle was the undoing of the sport’s most prolific figure, Shohei Ohtani. The best two-way player in baseball, inside his category of one, showed signs of breaking down in the latter portion of the season. First injuries forced him to stop pitching. Then he went homerless from late August until Thursday. Ohtani said it was only his ability, not injuries, holding him back, but he was dropped to sixth in the batting order for Game 3, and that doesn’t happen to an elite player in his prime unless there are issues. In the seventh inning of Game 4, with Kiké Hernández 90ft away from tying the game at five, Ohtani waved at an Ashby slider that was closer to Fresno than the Dodger Stadium home plate. Ohtani, the four-time MVP, wasn’t alone. Former MVP Mookie Betts hit light; former MVP Freddy Freeman hit even lighter. The lineup, collectively, hit for a .590 OPS in the series, while the pitching was uneven at best. After the game, manager Dave Roberts, who was out-skippered by Murphy all series, told Fox that “the great thing about what we do is, you can try as much as you want, want it as bad and there’s nothing you can do about it. There’s nothing guaranteed.” And that, it seems, gets to the heart of where we are with the Dodgers and where we may be with baseball: nothing, at all, is guaranteed. Not even after signing Kyle Tucker and Edwin Díaz in the offseason for a combined $309m. Not even after trading for Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal at the deadline. And not after writing $340m worth of checks. The Dodgers’ payroll is more than the combined payroll of the Rays, the Guardians, and the Brewers, the club that sent home “the team that destroyed baseball”. And so the Dodgers, always in the headlines, leave us with all sorts of questions. The most straightforward: how will they respond and retool? The bigger questions: can critics say they destroyed baseball when the Brewers and their 19th-ranked payroll just destroyed them? Is baseball, a game that involves both skill and luck and always keeps us guessing, really some kind of utopian paradise where paupers can actually compete for prizes against princes? Are high payrolls and all-star laden rosters the most important metrics when it comes to who can compete for a title? How much can a smart, deliberate team brass make up for small budgets? In other words: who can find the gamers, when they can’t afford the Hall of Famers?
